name: PCI Express 6.0
bandwidth_basis: x16, PER DIRECTION. CORRECTED IN AUDIT: the previous value (128) was half the RAW line rate (256 GB/s), but raw rate ignores the FLIT framing and FEC overhead that every real PCIe 6.0 transfer pays. PCIe 6.0 signals at 64 GT/s with PAM4 (2 bits/symbol) = 128 Gb/s raw per lane; applying 242B/256B framing gives 121 Gb/s of payload per lane, and 16 lanes = 1,936 Gb/s = 242 GB/s per direction, the figure PCI-SIG publishes. NOTE NVIDIA's own Blackwell Ultra datasheet prints 'PCIe Gen6: 256 GB/s' - that is the BIDIRECTIONAL AGGREGATE (2 x 242 would be 484, so it is in fact the raw double-wide figure); do not read it as a per-direction rate.
topology: Point-to-point host-to-device, up to 16 lanes, with flit-level framing and signalling changes versus PCIe 5.0. Shares the physical layer with CXL 4.0.
switching: Optional PCIe switch fabric, as for PCIe 5.0 - store-and-forward, no in-network compute.
notes: Inference consequence: at 128 GB/s per direction x16, a PCIe 6.0 host link is roughly 3.5x the per-direction rate of PCIe 5.0 but still about 3.5x below NVLink 4 per direction, so it does not change the guidance in pcie-gen5 - a tensor-parallel plan sized on PCIe 6.0 is still fabric-bound. The encoding change is the real risk: PAM4/FLIT and the retired receiver-sensitivity margin make Gen6 a materially different SI and retimer problem from Gen5, and NVIDIA's own comparison language treats PCIe Gen6 as the yardstick NVLink-C2C beats by 3.5x on area efficiency. Revision currency: PCI Express Base Specification Revisions 7.1 and 6.5 are both dated 2026-09-17 on the PCI-SIG index, so PCIe 6.0 is a shipped generation, not a preview. Confidence is deliberately low - the number is arithmetic from the line rate, and should be re-verified against the Base Specification x16 payload table before use.
